title: Motion on a sales page
excerpt: Use one motion to explain a change of state. A sales page that moves everywhere makes the buyer wait, so ship a still version for reduced motion.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. The slow bloom of ink fits a piece about motion that should explain one change and then stop.
caption: One change, then still. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How much animation belongs on a landing page?
faqs.answer: One meaningful motion is usually enough. It should explain a change of state, such as a menu opening or a step becoming current. A page that fades, slides, and parallax-scrolls every block asks the buyer to wait for the offer. The offer should be readable with the motion turned off.

faqs.question: What should happen when someone prefers reduced motion?
faqs.answer: Show the still page. Do not play a slower version of the same animation. Headlines, buttons, and explanations are present immediately. The W3C's WCAG principles include operable content, and a page that only reveals itself through motion is hard to operate for people who need it to stop.

faqs.question: Can motion hurt performance?
faqs.answer: Yes. web.dev's good threshold for Interaction to Next Paint is 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift should be 0.1 or less. Animation that blocks the main thread makes taps feel late, and animation that moves content without a request makes the page jump. Measure on a phone, not only in a desktop preview.

markdown:
One motion can explain a change of state. A sales page that moves in every section asks the buyer to wait for the offer. Used with restraint, animation on landing pages should earn that wait or get out of the way. Respect the request for reduced motion by shipping a still version that already makes sense.

The sentence is the sale. "This is what it does, and this is how to talk to us." If that sentence is gated behind a load-in, a scroll trigger, and a looping background, you have composed a trailer. Some people will watch. The person who came to decide will feel held hostage.

## One job for the motion you keep

Choose the change that is hard to understand in a still frame. A menu opening. A step in a sequence becoming the current step. A panel that was collapsed and is now open. The motion tells the eye where to look after their action. It connects cause and effect.

Everything else can appear. Headlines, prices, proofs, and forms do not need to rise into place. They need to be there. Entrance animations on every block as the page scrolls turn reading into a queue. The buyer scrolls, waits, reads a fragment, and scrolls again. You have added time without adding information.

Keep the duration short when you do animate. A state change is a glance, not a scene. If you can watch the animation as a piece of cinema, it is too long for a control. The button should feel responsive. The explanation should still be in the text, so a person who misses the motion, or pauses it, still has the meaning.

Looping motion in a hero is the habit to question first. A gradient that never settles, a three-dimensional object that spins, a video of hands typing: these ask for attention on every frame. They also compete with the words on top of them. If the loop is the brand, give it a still poster and let it run only when it does not obscure the offer and only when the visitor has not asked for quiet.

## Reduced motion is the first version

Build the still page, then add motion as an enhancement. That order matters. If the still page is an empty stage and the meaning lives in the timeline, you cannot honor a reduced-motion setting without deleting the pitch. The pitch has to exist as HTML.

When the operating system says the person prefers reduced motion, do less. Show the end state. Skip the parallax. Do not translate "reduced" into "the same spin, slower." Slow motion can be worse for the people the setting is meant to protect. The page should be complete and calm.

This sits inside a broader access standard. The W3C's WCAG 2 overview groups requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles, and W3C encourages WCAG 2.2. A control the person cannot reach, or a sale they cannot read unless they tolerate animation, fails the operable idea in plain sight. You do not need a motion manifesto. You need the setting to change what the page does.

Test it. On a phone and on a laptop, turn the preference on, reload, and read the page. Tab to the button. Confirm nothing essential is at zero opacity, off-screen, or waiting for a scroll event that will now never "count." Those bugs hide in the implementation of entrance effects. The still version is how you find them.

## What motion does to the tap and the layout

web.dev treats Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift as core measures of experience. A good INP is 200 milliseconds or less. A good CLS is 0.1 or less. Both are judged at the 75th percentile, split by mobile and desktop. A landing page that animates everything can miss both, even when the design file looked smooth on a new laptop.

INP suffers when animation and script work occupy the main thread at the moment someone taps. The tap is late. They tap again. The second tap hits the thing that just moved. You have built a bug out of polish. Heavy libraries, scroll listeners on every section, and large layout animations are the usual cause. Animate transform and opacity if you animate at all. Leave width, height, and top alone. Those trigger layout, and layout is how the page gets slow and unstable together.

CLS suffers when content flies in and pushes other content down, or when a late animation reserves a different box than the final one. Reserve the space. The button should not jump because a picture decided to arrive with a bounce. Movement that follows a tap, because the person opened something, is a different case from movement that happens while they are trying to read.

The Motion library can express a spring and a fade cleanly, and it can read the reduced-motion preference so the still path is the same component. That is a good use. It is not a reason to wrap every heading. A dependency that exists to move four things will be used to move forty unless the review is strict. Keep the allowed motions on a short list in the project.

## What to put on the short list

Write the allowed motions down where the code lives. A useful list is short enough to remember. The menu may animate its open and close. A disclosure may fade its panel. Nothing else moves on its own. Scroll does not trigger entrances. The hero does not loop. If a new section wants an exception, it has to name the change of state it is explaining, and the still version has to carry the same meaning.

Time the exception. If the motion runs longer than a glance, it is a scene, and scenes belong in a video the person chose to play. Springs and custom curves are easy to overuse because they feel crafted in isolation. Watch them next to the sentence they accompany. If you notice the curve, it is competing with the offer. Ease out quickly and be done.

Keep motion off the confirmation, the error, and the price. Those moments are decisions. They should change by content, not by choreography. A price that counts up from zero looks like a game and makes the number harder to trust. Show the number. If the number has a condition, write the condition beside it.

## The sales sentence does not wait

Put the offer in the first screen without an intro. Logo animations that play before the headline, full-screen loaders that exist only because the loader was designed, cookie-like bars that slide up over the button: each one delays the decision. The person gave you the visit. Start the visit.

Do not tie the appearance of the price, the proof, or the form to a scroll percentage. Some visitors jump straight to the button. Some use find-in-page. Some follow a link to a section. A reveal that assumes a slow, linear scroll fails all three. If a section is in the document, it should be readable when it is in view, and it should be in the document immediately.

Autoplaying carousels are a special case of the same mistake. They move the proof while the person is trying to read it, they are hard to operate, and they hide all but one item. A static row, or a row the person moves on purpose, respects the reader. If you have five logos or three quotes, show the ones you mean. Rotation is not editing.

Sound is almost never right on a sales page that loaded from a search result or an ad. If a video is the explanation, give it a poster, a control, and captions. Let them start it. Their ears may already be in a meeting.

## How to review a landing page that moves

Watch someone else use the page with the sound of your own explanation turned off. Do not tell them to scroll slowly. See whether they can state the offer, and whether they wait, annoyed, for a block to finish arriving. If they wait, remove that entrance.

Then do the mechanical pass. Reduced motion on. Keyboard only. A mid-range phone with a cold load. Tap the primary action during the first second. It should respond. The layout should not shift under the tap. If the only way to make the scores look good is to delete the motion, the motion was never carrying the sale.

Keep a before-and-after in the repository: the still component and the enhanced one. Future edits will "improve" the animation until it covers the sentence again. A short note next to the component, "this is the one motion, it explains the menu, the still state is the default under reduced motion," is enough governance for a small team.

Hanabi uses that order on marketing pages. The readable page is the deliverable. Motion is added where it explains a change, with a still path beside it. The craft is in the restraint, and the restraint is what makes the page feel finished instead of performed.

When you want that standard applied to a page that currently will not sit still, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the URL. The first question is which single motion is doing a job.

After they act, the page has a different job: tell them what happened. [The page after a form submits](/blog/the-page-after-a-form-submits) is the next piece, because a careful landing page can still waste the visit with a vague thank-you.
